definition.text: The branch of game theory that studies games in which groups of players can form coalitions and make binding agreements, enforced from outside, for example by contract law.

facts.text: Non-cooperative games, by contrast, allow no alliances or only agreements that enforce themselves, such as through credible threats.
Analysis focuses on which coalitions can form, what they can do jointly and the collective payoffs that result.
The main assumption is that all players form one grand coalition; the question is then how to divide its total payoff among them.
Researchers have proposed different solution concepts, such as the core and the Shapley value, based on different ideas of fairness.
Cooperative game theory has been proposed as a strategic theory of the firm, with different solutions mimicking different institutions.

definition.text: In a cooperative game, the function that gives the total payoff each possible coalition of players can secure by joining together.

facts.text: A cooperative game is specified simply by giving a value for every coalition, with the empty coalition worth zero.
Characteristic functions are often assumed superadditive: two separate coalitions together are worth at least the sum of their separate values.
In a simple game every coalition is either winning (worth 1) or losing (worth 0).

definition.text: The von Neumann–Morgenstern solution: the first solution concept proposed for cooperative games with more than two players, built on which allocations a coalition would object to.

facts.text: One allocation dominates another if some coalition prefers it and could obtain at least its members' payoffs on its own.
A stable set may not exist, is usually not unique and is hard to find, which spurred the development of other solution concepts.
The core is contained in every stable set.

definition.text: The allocation of a cooperative game that makes the largest complaints of coalitions, measured by what each could gain by leaving, as small as possible.

facts.text: The nucleolus is always unique.
If the core is non-empty, the nucleolus lies inside it.

definition.text: The extra surplus a coalition creates beyond what its smaller sub-coalitions already create.

facts.text: John Harsanyi used it in 1963 to generalize the Shapley value.

definition.text: A cooperative game with a 'snowballing' property, formally a supermodular characteristic function, introduced by Shapley in 1971.

facts.text: Convex games are totally balanced: their core, and the core of every subgame, is non-empty.
Similar results for submodular functions appear in combinatorial optimization.

definition.text: A simultaneous game in which players earn more when they choose the same course of action as one another.

facts.text: It has several pure-strategy Nash equilibria in which players choose matching strategies, and each player's best move depends on what they expect the other to do.
Choosing which side of the road to drive on is the typical example: a shared standard that saves lives if widely followed.
When it does not matter which option is picked as long as both pick the same, it is a pure coordination game.
Coordination games also have a mixed equilibrium, but it is worse for both than either pure equilibrium and is not evolutionarily stable.
They are closely tied to positive network externalities, the benefit of being in the same network as others.
The stag hunt, or assurance game, is a coordination game where the best joint outcome needs trust, while a safer option needs none.

title: Battle of the sexes

definition.text: A coordination game with conflicting interests: both players prefer doing the same thing over going alone but disagree on which thing to do.

facts.text: The standard story is a couple arguing over what to do at the weekend.
A round of cheap talk before play may let the players pick one of its several equilibria and earn more than without communication.

notes: No page of its own crawled; defined in Coordination game § Examples and used on Cheap talk.

definition.text: A de facto standard that people adopt freely, the typical social-science solution to a coordination problem.

facts.text: Such standards tend to be stable where everyone gains, but only by making mutually consistent choices.
A standard enforced by law (a de jure obligation standard) is instead a solution to a prisoner's-dilemma-type problem.

definition.text: An equilibrium that people tend to settle on when they must coordinate without talking, because it stands out for some reason.

facts.text: An equilibrium may stand out by paying more, being more salient, fairer or safer.
These reasons can clash, as in the stag hunt, where hunting stag together pays more but hunting hare is safer.

definition.text: The common outcome in which players end up at a worse equilibrium because they pick the safer option instead of the one paying most.

facts.text: Players are more likely to fail to coordinate on the risky option when its extra reward over the safe option is small.
Laboratory results suggest coordination failure is common in stag-hunt and order-statistic games.
In one weak-link experiment groups first failed to coordinate, but about 80% coordinated successfully when the game was repeated.

definition.text: A game in which choosing the same action as others creates a cost rather than a benefit, as under negative externalities.

facts.text: Chicken (hawk–dove) is the best-known two-player example.
In a crowding game each player's payoff falls as more others choose the same strategy, as when extra cars slow a road for everyone; a congestion game is a crowding game in networks.
In a discoordination game one player wants to match and the other to mismatch, so the only equilibrium is mixed; matching pennies is the classic case.

definition.text: In a cooperative game, the set of allocations from which no group of players could do better by breaking away from the whole group.

facts.text: A coalition blocks an allocation if its members could create more value on their own than they are given.
The core corresponds to situations where cooperation among all players can be kept going.
The idea appeared in Edgeworth's 1881 writing as the contract curve; the modern definition is due to Donald B. Gillies and Lloyd Shapley.
The core is always well defined but can be empty; the Bondareva–Shapley theorem says it is non-empty exactly when the game is 'balanced'.
In a game of 1000 left-shoe and 1001 right-shoe owners, the core gives the scarce left-shoe owners everything and right-shoe owners nothing.
Critics note how extremely sensitive the core is to an oversupply of one type of player.
Every Walrasian (competitive market) equilibrium lies in the core, though not every core allocation is a market equilibrium.
